strengths: Well-motivated empirical finding: Clear demonstration that text conditions fail for robotic control with excellent cross-attention visualizations (Figure 3) showing poor word-region grounding in simulated environments
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 3 benchmarks (12 tasks) with consistent improvements and multiple strong baselines (both task-agnostic and task-adaptive methods)
Thorough ablation studies including component analysis (Table 4), layer selection (Table 5), timestep ablation (Appendix A.1), and frame-wise attention visualizations (Figure 6)
Straightforward and technically sound approach using behavior cloning loss to learn task and visual prompts without fine-tuning the diffusion model
Strong empirical results: state-of-the-art on MetaWorld (95.2 vs 93.1 prior SOTA) and consistent gains across all benchmarks with reasonable standard deviations
Good presentation with clear motivation, informative figures, logical flow, and implementation details enabling reproducibility
Practical solution addressing real limitation of task-agnostic visual representations for robotic control
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core components (learnable prompts, vision encoder features as conditions, behavior cloning) are well-established techniques from prior work (CoOp, SD4Match, EcoDepth). The contribution is primarily in combining existing methods rather than proposing new mechanisms

Insufficient justification of critical design choices: No comparison of vision encoders (why DINOv2?), limited justification for dense vs. global features, arbitrary prompt lengths (lt=4, lv=16) without ablation, and variable timestep performance across tasks (Table 6)

Shallow analysis of text condition failure: Attribution to 'domain gap' is intuitive but not rigorously investigated. No experiments with domain-specific text, sensitivity to VLM choice (Gemini 2.5) unexplored, and null condition's <eos> grounding deserves deeper investigation

Experimental design concerns: Large standard deviations on some tasks (Cheetah-run: ±8.4), only 3 seeds (insufficient for robustness), fairness of comparing image-domain methods (CoOp/TADP) to control tasks, and unexplained discrepancy in SCR baseline performance

Limited analysis of learned representations: No visualization or interpretation of task prompts, no ablation on initialization sensitivity, no evaluation of transfer across similar tasks, and unclear what visual prompts actually capture

Significant computational overhead: 48ms latency vs 26ms for SCR (~85% increase), inconsistent statements about parameter counts, and inference cost implications for real-time robotic control not adequately discussed
Incremental empirical gains on several tasks: Some improvements marginally exceed noise (Finger-spin: 68.0 vs 66.9), large error bar overlaps with baselines reduce significance of differences

Generalization limitations: All experiments in simulation only with no real robot validation; unclear how many demonstrations required to learn prompts; no evaluation of task transfer or sim-to-real applicability

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clear demonstration that text prompts fail in robotic control (Figure 3), attributable to domain gap between web images and simulated environments, with insightful cross-attention visualizations explaining poor grounding

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Consistent improvements across 12 tasks on three standard benchmarks (DMC, MetaWorld, Adroit) with proper ablations (Tables 4-5), multiple seeds, and strong baselines including recent methods (VC-1, SCR)

Thorough analysis and interpretability: Cross-attention maps effectively visualize prompt behavior; Appendix A.3 provides additional insight on null condition tokens; Figure 6 demonstrates frame-level dynamics of learned prompts
Practical simplicity: Straightforward method using learnable embeddings and vision encoder features without complex auxiliary optimization procedures, potentially useful for practitioners
Strong empirical results: State-of-the-art performance across all 12 tasks with mean improvements of 6.0 (DMC), 11.1 (MetaWorld), and 7.3 (Adroit) percentage points over prior work
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: Combines existing techniques (learnable prompts from CoOp, vision encoder conditioning from SD4Match/EcoDepth) without substantial innovation; main contribution is application to robotic control with empirical observation that text fails

Unjustified hyperparameter choices: Task token length (4), visual token length (16), and compression dimension (48) appear arbitrary with no ablations; timestep choice (t=0) not thoroughly justified beyond empirical performance in Table 6

Vision encoder not ablated: Only DINOv2 tested; unclear whether improvements stem from the conditioning approach or DINOv2's representation quality; comparison to CLIP, MoCo, or other self-supervised encoders missing

Weak baseline selection: CoOp and TADP designed for classification/segmentation, not control; text baselines rely on Gemini-generated captions without testing hand-crafted prompts or exploring prompt engineering

Significant efficiency overhead insufficiently addressed: 48ms latency versus 26ms (SCR) and 11ms (VC-1)—~2x slowdown critical for real-time robotic control; efficiency penalty relegated to appendix despite practical importance

Limited scope and theoretical contribution: Evaluation restricted to simulation only (no real robots); some tasks at ceiling (100% success); lacks mechanistic understanding of why task+visual prompts work or which diffusion properties enable robotic control
Statistical rigor gaps: No significance testing despite overlapping error bars (e.g., Finger-spin: ORCA 68.0±1.0 vs TADP 66.9±0.2); no corrections for multiple comparisons
Incomplete domain gap analysis: If <eos> token already grounds well (Appendix A.3), why is additional prompt structure essential? Main paper insufficiently addresses this apparent contradiction

strengths: Well-motivated problem identification: Clear demonstration that text conditions fail in robotic control through cross-attention visualization analysis, with domain gap explanation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 12 tasks across 3 benchmarks with thorough ablations, layer analysis, and additional experiments on different backbones and encoders
Strong empirical results: State-of-the-art performance (74.3 DMC, 95.2 MetaWorld, 65.3 Adroit) with good parameter efficiency (10.6M learnable parameters)
Simple and practical solution: Elegantly straightforward approach without complex optimization, making it easy to implement and adapt
Thorough analysis and visualization: Cross-attention maps, efficiency comparisons, and ablation studies provide good interpretability of learned representations
Clear presentation and logical flow: Well-structured narrative from motivation through analysis to comprehensive evaluation
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Combines existing techniques (learnable implicit prompts from CoOp, visual features from TADP/SD4Match) without methodological innovation; primarily an application contribution
Strong architectural dependency: Results specific to Stable Diffusion v1.5; DiT-based SD 3.0 achieves only 30 mean score vs 65.3 for SD 1.5, limiting generalizability to future architectures
Hyperparameter choices lack principled justification: Token lengths (4 task, 16 visual), timestep selection (t=0), and layer selection determined empirically without theoretical grounding
Limited analysis of learned representations: Cross-attention visualizations for only one task; unclear what visual features are captured or whether task prompts transfer between similar tasks
Restricted experimental scope: Simulation-only evaluation (no real robots), very low demonstration counts (2-5), homogeneous MuJoCo environments, limited multi-task analysis (in appendix)
Incomplete baseline comparisons: Vision-Language-Action models mentioned but not empirically compared; claims about their expensive fine-tuning not validated
Insufficient theoretical insight: Why learnable tokens outperform text beyond domain gap? Why is frame-level conditioning important? Properties of diffusion models for control?
Technical clarity gaps: Exact mechanism of prompt concatenation in text encoder, projection layer architecture, prompt initialization strategy not clearly specified

strengths: Clear problem identification with strong empirical analysis: Paper effectively demonstrates why text conditions fail in robotic control through cross-attention visualization analysis, providing valuable insights for the community

Comprehensive experimental validation: Consistent improvements across 12 tasks on three diverse benchmarks (DMC, MetaWorld, Adroit) with proper statistical reporting (3 seeds with standard deviations)
Thorough ablation studies: Component analysis, layer selection, vision encoder choices, timestep ablations, and comparisons with fine-tuning provide strong experimental support for design decisions
Parameter efficiency with practical design: Only 10.6M learnable parameters versus 302.3M for full fine-tuning, enabling task-specific adaptation without storing multiple models
Excellent presentation and visualization: Figures effectively communicate intuitions; cross-attention maps provide interpretability into what the model learns
Extended evaluation on diverse tasks: LIBERO-Long evaluation demonstrates applicability to long-horizon language-conditioned tasks; additional comparisons with state-of-the-art encoders (Table E)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Learnable prompts follow CoOp [70] and visual conditioning follows TADP [32]. Core contribution is primarily the application to robotic control and empirical finding about text condition failure rather than methodological innovation

Architecture-specific findings with poor generalization: Evaluation restricted to Stable Diffusion v1.5; SD 3.0 (DiT) performs 2× worse (30.0 vs 65.3), and video diffusion models fail substantially. Limits future applicability as architectures evolve
Significant inference overhead: 48ms latency versus 11-26ms for baselines (4× slower than VC-1), limiting practical deployment. This overhead not adequately discussed in main paper

Insufficient analysis of learned representations: Limited interpretation of what task/visual prompts encode; no analysis of prompt transferability across tasks or visualization of prompt evolution during training

Incomplete justification of design choices: DINOv2 selection not well motivated (only Table C ablation); dense vs. global visual features claimed but not empirically justified; token lengths (lt=4, lv=16) appear arbitrary

Limited evaluation scope and scalability: All simulations only (no real robots); small demonstration datasets (2-5) with no analysis of scaling; missing comparisons with recent Vision-Language-Action models; unclear how method generalizes to different embodiments

Reproducibility concerns: Code availability not mentioned; reliance on proprietary Gemini 2.5 for caption generation; some implementation details relegated to appendix; compression layer design appears ad-hoc

Lack of theoretical understanding: Paper is primarily empirical without theoretical justification for why learnable prompts fundamentally outperform text; no analysis of optimization landscape or convergence properties

Incomplete experimental design and analysis: No investigation of when text conditions might be preferable; no failure case analysis; bias potential from online evaluation intervals not discussed; interaction between prompt learning and frozen diffusion model not deeply analyzed
